title: G-D-L
hook: gadol, gedulah: great, and to grow

segments.voice: Yesterday, P-Sh-T: peshat, the plain sense, the floor every reading stands on. Your line was plain. Did you hear what someone actually said? Today, a new week, and a root about size. Day one thousand four hundred one.

Pencil marks climb a kitchen doorframe, each one with a name and a date. Nobody saw the child get taller between the marks. It happened at night, at school, over cereal. Then one day the mark is above the parent's shoulder. In Hebrew, the word for that kind of growing and the word for great are the same root. Gadal, he grew. Gadol, great, big. A gadol can be a grown-up, or a towering teacher. Being great and getting bigger, in this language, are one family of words. Today's root: gimel, dalet, lamed. G-D-L.
screen: `MARKS ON A DOORFRAME.` → `GADAL: HE GREW.` → `G-D-L: GREAT, AND TO GROW.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the child. When Isaac, the long-awaited son, gets bigger, the Torah marks it simply: "And the child grew, and was weaned." And Abraham throws a great feast. Same root, twice in one verse: the child grows, the feast is great. Growing is worth celebrating. Second, the promise. Earlier, God promises Abraham, "I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and be thou a blessing." Notice where the sentence lands. Not on great. On blessing. Some readers hear in it that being made great is for the sake of being a blessing. Third, the grown-up. In Exodus, Moses is raised in Pharaoh's palace, and then the text says: "when Moses was grown up, that he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." Grown up, there, is from this root. And what the grown Moses does, in the story, is step outside and look at someone else's load. Growing up, in this verse, looks outward. Fourth, the prayer. The Kaddish, said in synagogue and by mourners, opens with this root: yitgadal, may God's name grow great. It's a strange thing to pray. Can God get bigger? Some teachers answer that the Kaddish asks for God's greatness to grow in the world, in how people see and live. And mourners say it in a season when their own world may seem to have grown smaller. So G-D-L holds a child, a promise, a grown man and a prayer. In every one, greatness isn't sitting still. It's growing, and it's pointed outward.
screen: `THE CHILD: AND THE CHILD GREW.` · `THE PROMISE: GREAT, TO BE A BLESSING.` · `THE GROWN-UP: HE LOOKED ON THEIR BURDENS.` · `THE PRAYER: YITGADAL.` · then, large: `גָּדַל`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help something grow. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your reach that's growing, or trying to. A plant on a windowsill. A child learning to read. A new coworker finding their feet. A friendship that needs one more conversation. Choose one. Picture the next small thing you could do for it. Water. Patience. A question. An introduction. Hold that one thing in mind, and imagine the next mark on the doorframe. If you pray, you can bring its name, or theirs, into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
G-D-L. Gimel, dalet, lamed: the root of gadal, to grow, and gadol, great, and of yitgadal, the first word of the Kaddish. Today's word.
Your line: grow. Today, do the one small thing you chose for the growing thing, and leave a mark somewhere to remember it. Day one thousand four hundred one.

howItsDone: The Kaddish, recited in synagogue services and by mourners, begins with yitgadal, from the root G-D-L, asking that God's name grow great; in Jewish speech a gadol can mean a great Torah scholar.

original.note: Hebrew: he grew, became great; gadol means great.

trapdoor: what you thought: great means important, and grow means taller.
what it means: in Hebrew, one root, G-D-L, holds both: great, and to grow.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 21:8 uses it twice — the child grew, and a great feast — and the Kaddish opens with yitgadal.
